fields.title: Polka: the report that reveals the buyer
fields.summary: A store owner identifies buyers from an "anonymized" report. There are 600 such stores.
fields.decisionPrompt: What do we do? State the price of your decision.
fields.brief/role: You are a product manager at Polka.
fields.brief/company: Polka is a fictional grocery delivery service from local stores: 900 partner stores, a buyer app, and a partner dashboard.
fields.brief/context: You are a product manager at Polka. A small store owner mentioned in a support chat: "I can see from the report that Marina bought her wine on Thursdays again." The report contains no names. The store is small—40–60 orders per week.
fields.brief/objective: Remove buyer identifiability from the report without taking away the tools the store relies on.
fields.brief/constraints: About 600 of the 900 stores are small—the report is their primary tool.
fields.brief/task: Decide what you are doing and what remains visible to the partner.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Anonymized data ceases to be anonymized at low volumes
fields.learnTakeaway/body: Removing names is not enough: in a sample of forty orders, order contents, day of the week, and repetition point to a specific person for someone who knows the customers personally. The test is simple—imagine the report in the hands of a small store owner. And it is better to solve this not by disabling features, but by separating them: operational data is needed for work, while identifiability is almost always introduced by an analytical layer built on top of it.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content: Orders by day with contents, amount, delivery district, and "frequent buyer" flag.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content: With 8 orders on Thursday and one containing wine, a frequent buyer is easily deduced by an owner who knows customers personally.
fields.evidenceCards/2/title: What else is in the report
fields.evidenceCards/2/content: Age group, order time, repetition frequency.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content: 900 total, of which about 600 are small stores with comparable volume.
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Zero work. Leave the report as is: it contains no names, data is formally anonymized.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence: risk remains with 600 stores. Known to us, which weakens our position during an investigation.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Remove the frequent buyer flag. One day.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence: removes the most direct hint. Contents and days remain, and identifiability persists at low volume. Half measure.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Aggregation threshold: detail only available above volume threshold
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: One week. Show item-level details only to stores with volume above the threshold, and aggregates to everyone else.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence: small stores see aggregates instead of individual orders. The report's value to them drops—and this represents 600 out of 900 partners.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Aggregation threshold plus preservation of operational view
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: One and a half weeks. Individual orders are visible in the operational section—needed for fulfillment; the analytical report with repetition and profiles is only available above the volume threshold.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence: operational work is unaffected, analytics with re-identification risk are restricted for low volumes.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Does not understand re-identification via a combination of attributes
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Does not apply an aggregation threshold
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Does not distinguish between data access levels
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Fails to consider that some data can be avoided collecting and showing
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Deletion and anonymization are treated as the same thing
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: Fails to consider what should be included in the data access log
